relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: David compares his cedar palace with the ark's fabric shelter.
Nathan blesses the royal impulse before listening deeply enough.
Night brings correction to the prophet.
David is told he will not build the Divine house.
Sacred presence remembers freedom to move from tent to tent.
The Divine never demanded cedar from Israel's shepherd-leaders.
David's story is recalled from sheep pasture to political rule.
Protection and fame are interpreted as gifts, not moral immunity.
The people are promised stable dwelling beyond repeated violence.
The oracle turns David's building plan around: YHWH will build David a house.
A son will continue the kingdom after David joins his ancestors.
The son, not the warrior father, will build the temple.
Royal covenant is spoken through parental intimacy and enduring love.
The dynasty is imagined as enduring inside Divine house and kingdom.
Nathan delivers the corrected word rather than protecting his first answer.
David sits before YHWH and asks who he and his house are.
He receives the long future as an overwhelming enlargement of grace.
Speech gives way before being fully known.
David attributes the promise to Divine purpose rather than his entitlement.
He confesses the uniqueness of YHWH.
Israel's redemption is praised through language that must still remember nations displaced by the story.
Covenant makes Israel a people called into enduring relationship.
David asks the dynastic word to stand.
He seeks a lasting name for YHWH through the endurance of his house.
The promise gives him courage to pray.
He trusts the goodness of the word spoken.
The prayer closes by receiving blessing as gift, never as immunity.

contemplative_note: Nathan's correction may be the chapter's most important prophetic act. The Divine refuses confinement in cedar and refuses David's assumption that royal desire equals sacred instruction. Covenant is not ownership of God, land, or future; it is a call for power to become shepherding, accountable, and open to correction.
